description: A case study brief from the Landscape Architecture Foundation's Landscape Performance Series on the Cheonggyecheon Stream Restoration Project in Seoul, South Korea, completed in 2005. The Seoul Metropolitan Government demolished an ageing elevated freeway that carried 169,000 vehicles a day and uncovered about 3.6 miles (5.84 km) of the historic stream, roughly 100 acres, at a total cost near $380 million, about $120 million of it landscape. Measures: 22 new bridges, connections to five subway lines and 18 bus lines, car use discouraged in the centre, over 4,200 meetings with business owners, and 120,000 tons a day of treated Han River and subway pump water to keep a 40 cm flow. Reported results include corridor temperatures 3.3 to 5.9 degrees C cooler than a parallel road four to seven blocks away, bird species up from 6 to 36, and about 22 trillion won ($1.98 billion) of redevelopment investment; keeping the freeway would have cost about $90 million in repairs. Lessons: accessibility for visually impaired and mobility-limited users was retrofitted later at higher cost. Coverage: one corridor in central Seoul. Access: free web brief; the figures are as reported by the foundation. It supports heat adaptation planning and assessment of public space redesign; related records are not yet linked.
